ng_2012.name: Transport-dispersive IgG capture model
ng_2012.description: The model describes human IgG capture from a feed by protein A chromatography using AbSolute, a silica-based adsorbent. It predicts time-dependent movement and adsorption of IgG and impurities through a packed column, including breakthrough and elution behavior. The model combines axial transport and dispersion, finite-rate mass transfer, and adsorption equilibrium, with a saturation-dependent empirical mass-transfer correlation. The authors used small-column pulse, pressure-flow, and breakthrough experiments to estimate parameters, then optimized batch operating conditions for productivity subject to yield, purity, and pressure constraints. They tested the optimized process experimentally with human polyclonal IgG and with an IgG–bovine serum model feed. The authors use the integrated approach to design a high-productivity capture process with fewer experiments, and report a verified productivity of 2.9 kg L⁻¹ day⁻¹.

facts.text: The model was developed for antibody capture using AbSolute, a novel silica-based high-performance protein A adsorbent.
facts.quote: a novel silica-based high performance protein A adsorbent called AbSolute

facts.text: The process example used human IgG as product and treated non-retained materials, including impurities, as a second pseudo-component.
facts.quote: the components involved were assumed to behave as two pseudo-components: IgG and impurities.

facts.text: AbSolute had an average particle diameter of 44 μm, a pore diameter of 1000 Å, and a specific surface area of 65 m² g⁻¹.
Breakthrough experiments used Tricorn columns 5 mm in diameter and 5 cm long.
facts.quote: Three sets of breakthrough experiments were performed in small-scale Tricorn columns of 5 mm diameter and 5 cm length

facts.text: The optimized process was verified in a column 5 mm in diameter and 8.5 cm long.
facts.quote: in a column of 5 mm diameter and 8.5 cm length

facts.text: Equilibration and washing used phosphate-buffered saline at pH 7.4, elution used 0.1 M glycine–HCl at pH 3, and regeneration used HCl at pH 1.5.
facts.quote: PBS, pH 7.4, was used for equilibration and wash. 0.1 M glycine–HCl, pH 3, and HCl, pH 1.5, were used for elution and regeneration, respectively.

facts.text: The authors describe the chromatography model as a lumped-parameter transport-dispersive model.
facts.quote: The transport-dispersive model is a lumped parameter model

facts.text: The model represents changing concentrations along the column and over time, with a mobile-phase mass balance and a stationary-phase adsorption kinetic equation.
The selected chromatography model has ten estimated parameters, and the process optimization adds the experimentally fitted apparent friction factor, giving eleven parameters overall.
facts.quote: In total, there were ten parameters in the selected transport-dispersive model

facts.text: The model was discretized by orthogonal collocation on finite elements and solved in C++ with the IDA solver from SUNDIALS.
The model represents axial dispersion using an empirical correlation based on the modified van Deemter relationship.
facts.quote: The apparent axial dispersion coefficient,  D_L, is in this work defined by an empirical correlation

facts.text: The model uses a variable lumped mass-transfer coefficient that changes empirically with the fraction of unoccupied binding sites.
IgG adsorption is represented by a Langmuir isotherm modified by pH, while impurity adsorption is represented by a linear isotherm.
The model assumes the same adsorption kinetics for IgG and impurities.
facts.quote: Adsorption kinetics was assumed to be the same for both IgG and the impurities

facts.text: Pulse tests injected 10 μl acetone at linear velocities from 100 to 1500 cm h⁻¹, with water as the mobile phase, and measured outlet absorbance at 280 nm.
facts.quote: Pulses of acetone (10 μl) were injected into the system with and without the column at linear velocities, u, of 100, 150, 300, 600 and 1500 cm h⁻¹ with water as the mobile phase

facts.text: Breakthrough experiments varied IgG feed concentration from 1 to 10 g L⁻¹ and linear velocity from 100 to 1500 cm h⁻¹ across three experimental sets.
Pressure-flow measurements used a 5 mm diameter, 20 cm column with PBS at pH 7.4 and velocities from 60 to 900 cm h⁻¹.
facts.quote: Column pressure drops (the differences between the system pressures with and without the column) were measured for a column of 5 mm diameter and 20 cm length, L, using phosphate buffered saline (PBS), pH 7.4, at linear velocities, u, of 60, 120, 150, 240, 300, 450, 600, 750 and 900 cm h⁻¹.

facts.text: Outlet solute concentrations were measured by absorbance at 280 nm, or at 300 nm when the 280 nm signal saturated.
facts.quote: Solute concentrations were measured at the column outlet by absorbance at 280 nm, or 300 nm in the case of signal saturation at 280 nm

facts.text: The optimized batch yield and purity were measured by protein A HPLC using a 4.6 mm diameter, 5 cm long analytical column with 20 μm particles.
facts.quote: Each analysis took 4.5 min using a Poros A 20 pre-packed protein A analytical column of 4.6 mm diameter and 5 cm length with 20 μm particles.

facts.text: Equilibrium binding capacities were estimated by integrating breakthrough curves using the trapezium rule rather than reading capacity at 50% breakthrough.
facts.quote: Area integration of the breakthrough curves was approximated by the trapezium rule.

facts.text: The saturation-dependent kinetic parameters were fitted simultaneously to breakthrough curves at different velocities using constrained optimization by linear approximation.
The pH-dependent equilibrium parameter was fitted to partial-breakthrough and elution data, using only the unsaturated experimental signal within 2 AU at 280 nm.
facts.quote: Only the unsaturated experimental signal, i.e. within 2 AU at 280 nm, was considered for parameter fitting due to the unreliability of the saturated signal.

facts.text: Reported parameter errors are one standard deviation where available, and statistical errors were only available for parameters estimated by least squares.
facts.quote: Errors in the estimated model parameters were determined statistically and are only available for the parameters estimated by a least squares' method.

facts.text: Fitting the kinetic parameters took 42 minutes of CPU time on two Intel Xeon E5520 processors at 2.26 GHz with 24 GB memory.
facts.quote: The determination of these kinetic parameters required a total of 42 min CPU time on two Intel Xeon E5520 processors of 2.26 GHz with 24.0 Gb memory.

facts.text: Optimization targeted productivity subject to minimum yield of 95%, minimum purity of 98%, and a maximum column pressure drop of either 1.0 or 2.5 bar.
The productivity optimization assumed 24-hour operation and held regeneration and equilibration volumes fixed at 4 column volumes each.
facts.quote: assuming 24 h operation. The regeneration and equilibration volumes (V_R and V_Q) were kept constant at 4 CV

facts.text: The optimization used a constant superficial velocity across loading, washing, elution, regeneration, and equilibration.
facts.quote: A constant superficial velocity for all the zones (i.e. loading, wash, elution, regeneration and equilibration) was calculated

facts.text: The selected optimum used a 5 mm diameter, 8.5 cm long column at 2000 cm h⁻¹, with 15.3 CV load, 2.8 CV wash, and 3.3 CV elution volumes.
The model predicted a maximum productivity of 2.9 kg L⁻¹ day⁻¹ for column lengths between 5 and 8.5 cm, independent of whether the maximum pressure drop was 1.0 or 2.5 bar.
The maximum predicted throughput was 5.2 g day⁻¹ for a 5 mm diameter, 10 cm long column operated at 2.5 bar.
At the optimized conditions, the human polyclonal IgG run achieved 99.4% yield and 99.6% purity, while the IgG–bovine serum feed run achieved 97.7% yield and 98.1% purity.
facts.quote: The yield and purity obtained for the experimental run with human polyclonal IgG were 99.4% and 99.6%, respectively, whereas those for the experimental run with the model feed were 97.7% and 98.1%, respectively.

facts.text: The optimized process was verified at an experimental column pressure drop of approximately 2.5 bar, and the authors concluded that the predicted productivity was feasible in practice.
The fitted kinetic parameters were reported to be inappropriate for predicting breakthrough below 300 cm h⁻¹, and the model fitted behavior above 60% breakthrough poorly.
At optimized high velocity, the simulation overestimated IgG breakthrough and product loss during loading, so simulated yield was lower than experimental yield.
facts.quote: Higher yields were obtained in the experimental batch run than in the simulation. This can be explained by the overestimated IgG breakthrough, i.e. overestimated product loss during loading

facts.text: The authors chose a lumped-parameter model over a general-rate model to reduce the number of parameters and experiments while retaining sufficient accuracy, following the rationale of Chan et al. (2008).
facts.quote: By selecting a lumped parameter model, as opposed to a general rate model, the number of key model parameters to be estimated, and thus the experimentation effort for parameter estimation, can be drastically reduced whilst still ensuring sufficient model accuracy

facts.text: The paper contrasts its model with the surface-layer model with pore diffusion of McCue et al. (2003) and the heterogeneous binding model of Perez-Almodovar and Carta (2009), which it describes as more complex alternatives.
facts.quote: The use of Eq. (6) enables more accurate breakthrough predictions in the absence of a complex model (such as the surface layer model with pore diffusion [6] and the heterogeneous binding model [10]).

facts.text: The estimated maximum IgG binding capacity exceeded the previously reported 37–69 g L⁻¹ range cited from McCue et al. (2003), Hahn et al. (2003), Hahn et al. (2005), and Perez-Almodovar and Carta (2009).
facts.quote: This may be related to the large specific surface area of AbSolute particles (65 m² g⁻¹) for ligand coupling.

facts.text: The paper reports that the AbSolute friction factor was of the same order of magnitude as the value reported for Prosep-vA Ultra by McCue et al. (2003), accounting for the adsorbents' different particle sizes.
The model was used to optimize batch-process productivity while enforcing yield, purity, and pressure-drop constraints.
facts.quote: The main drawback of such an approach is the lack of flexibility to predict and consider process yield and purity as direct constraints in the optimization problem.

facts.text: The integrated experimental, estimation, optimization, and verification approach took 75 person-hours, or approximately two weeks, for the AbSolute example.
facts.quote: the capture of antibody by AbSolute in a batch column to be optimized in 75 person-hours.

facts.text: The authors estimate that the integrated approach reduced the expensive, labor-intensive experimentation required for process optimization by two- to five-fold.
facts.quote: Expensive and labor-intensive experimentation, and thus time and costs, required for process optimization were drastically reduced by an estimate of two to five folds.
